overview.summary:
The field of CNN-based image classification on Fashion-MNIST is well-established, with reported test accuracies ranging from ~88% for simple architectures to near 99.65% for optimized, augmented models. Data augmentation — including flips, translations, rotations, and more exotic methods — is broadly shown to improve generalization, reduce overfitting, and push accuracy higher, particularly when training data is limited or the model is small. The literature consistently demonstrates that even basic geometric augmentations (the focus of this experiment) provide measurable accuracy gains over unaugmented baselines.

However, the field increasingly moves beyond simple augmentations toward advanced strategies (Mixup, CutMix, AutoAugment) and larger architectures (ResNets, ViTs), making it harder to isolate the specific contribution of simple augmentation on small CNNs. Most published work does not run controlled two-condition experiments with fixed seeds, making direct comparisons across studies difficult. This experiment's controlled design — holding architecture, optimizer, and hyperparameters fixed while varying only augmentation — directly addresses a gap in reproducible, minimal-footprint benchmarking on Fashion-MNIST.
open_problems: Isolating the contribution of individual augmentation types (e.g., flips vs. rotations vs. translations) without confounding from other design choices
Determining how augmentation benefits scale with model size — whether small CNNs benefit more or less than larger architectures
Lack of standardized controlled experiments: most papers vary multiple factors simultaneously, making attribution of accuracy gains to augmentation alone difficult
Reproducibility across random seeds is rarely reported with more than one or two seeds, leaving statistical reliability of results unclear
Optimal augmentation magnitude (degree of rotation, translation range) is dataset- and architecture-dependent and rarely systematically searched for simple CNNs
Generalization from benchmark datasets like Fashion-MNIST to real-world fashion images remains a persistent gap
Whether gains from simple augmentations plateau quickly with more training epochs, and whether 5 epochs is sufficient to observe the full effect

gaps.approach: Extract per-class precision, recall, F1, and full confusion matrices from augmented and non-augmented trained models across seeds 42 and 123 (four models total). gaps.question: Does basic image augmentation disproportionately improve or reduce accuracy on specific Fashion-MNIST garment classes, particularly for morphologically similar or asymmetric classes?
gaps.why_open: (Yee 2026) notes that morphologically distinctive categories such as trousers, bags, and footwear show high discriminative performance but does not study how augmentation changes per-class accuracy. All papers reporting augmentation effects on Fashion-MNIST (Greeshma et al. 2019; Mukhamediev 2024; Hassan et al. 2025; Kayed et al. 2020) aggregate accuracy into a single number, obscuring which garment classes drive gains or losses. (Agarwal et al. 2025) found that augmentation did not consistently improve accuracy for the best-performing model on CIFAR-10, suggesting class-level heterogeneity, but no analogous per-class study exists for Fashion-MNIST. Fashion-MNIST has known confusable class pairs such as T-shirt versus shirt versus pullover where flip-induced distortions might introduce label-ambiguous training examples and hurt recognition.
gaps.hypothesis: Augmentation will disproportionately help symmetric garment classes (trousers, pullovers, coats) for which horizontal flips are valid invariances, while potentially reducing accuracy for fine-grained confusable classes such as shirt versus T-shirt/top where flipped images introduce label ambiguity.
gaps.data_needed: Fashion-MNIST test set (10,000 images, 10 balanced classes); predictions from the four trained models produced in the core experiment.

log.text: Drafting the research plan for the chosen gap

risks.risk: With only 2 seeds, per-class accuracy differences may fall within random seed noise and the symmetry hypothesis cannot be confirmed or rejected with confidence.
risks.mitigation: Explicitly frame all per-class findings as exploratory throughout the paper; focus interpretation only on effects exceeding 1.5x the binomial standard error (~1.5pp at p=0.90); report the full seed-level range alongside the mean for every class; recommend additional seeds as future work in the Discussion section.

risks.risk: SmallCNN trained for only 5 epochs may not converge to sufficient accuracy to reveal differential class-level augmentation effects above the noise floor.
risks.mitigation: The specified architecture (3 conv blocks, BatchNorm, Dropout) is well-validated for Fashion-MNIST and expected to achieve 88-93% overall in 5 epochs; if overall accuracy is below 85%, add a dedicated caveat paragraph in Results noting that class-level conclusions may be confounded by under-training.

risks.risk: Fashion-MNIST product images may already be horizontally standardized, making horizontal flip a valid invariance for all 10 classes including hypothesized asymmetric items (shirts, ankle boots), rendering the symmetry hypothesis untestable.
risks.mitigation: Inspect sample_augmented_images.png from T1.2 to characterize actual flip effects on asymmetric classes; report empirical confusion matrix findings regardless of whether they confirm or refute the morphological hypothesis; the delta confusion matrix will reveal augmentation effects even if the symmetry annotation is imprecise.

risks.risk: GPU training run crashes or produces corrupted checkpoints, requiring re-execution and wasting GPU time.
risks.mitigation: Save checkpoints after every epoch (not just the best) to enable recovery from any epoch; validate checkpoint integrity in T3.1 by cross-checking test accuracy against the corresponding training log final-epoch val_acc within a 3pp tolerance.

tasks.description: Download Fashion-MNIST train (60,000) and test (10,000) splits via torchvision.datasets.FashionMNIST. Define two transform pipelines: (1) no_aug using ToTensor and Normalize(mean=0.2860, std=0.3530); (2) aug using RandomHorizontalFlip(p=0.5), RandomAffine(degrees=10, translate=(0.1,0.1)), ToTensor, and Normalize(mean=0.2860, std=0.3530). Create a 90/10 train/val split (54,000/6,000) using torch.utils.data.random_split with a generator seeded per run. Save dataset statistics to dataset_stats.json and save a grid of sample images under both pipelines for visual verification.

tasks.description: Implement a SmallCNN class in PyTorch with three convolutional blocks (Conv2d->BatchNorm2d->ReLU->MaxPool2d(2,2)) with channel progression 1->32->64->128 using 3x3 kernels and padding=1, followed by Flatten->Linear(128*3*3, 256)->ReLU->Dropout(0.5)->Linear(256, 10). Implement a set_seed(seed) function that seeds Python random, numpy, torch, and torch.cuda.manual_seed_all for full reproducibility, and sets torch.backends.cudnn.deterministic=True. Save the implementation to model.py and print total parameter count to model_summary.txt.

tasks.description: Implement a train_epoch() function using Adam(lr=0.001, betas=(0.9,0.999)) and CrossEntropyLoss with batch_size=128 that returns per-epoch train loss and accuracy. Implement an evaluate() function that returns loss, overall accuracy, and a DataFrame of (sample_idx, true_label, pred_label, prob_0..prob_9) for any DataLoader. Implement a run_training() wrapper that executes exactly 5 epochs, logs per-epoch metrics (epoch, train_loss, train_acc, val_loss, val_acc) to a CSV, saves the best checkpoint by val_acc, and also saves epoch-wise checkpoints for crash recovery. methods.purpose: Random horizontal flip (p=0.5) plus RandomAffine(degrees=10, translate=(0.1,0.1)) applied only at training time in the augmentation condition to test whether simple geometric invariances improve generalization.

methods.name: Per-class classification metrics via scikit-learn
methods.purpose: Computation of per-class precision, recall, F1, support, and accuracy (correct/1000) to decompose aggregate accuracy into class-level signals revealing which garment categories drive gains or losses.

methods.name: Confusion matrix delta analysis
methods.purpose: Row-normalized 10x10 confusion matrices averaged across seeds per condition; delta matrix (aug minus no_aug) identifies class-pair confusions that are amplified or reduced by augmentation.

metrics.name: Per-class test accuracy
metrics.definition: For each of the 10 Fashion-MNIST classes c: accuracy_c = (number of test images of class c correctly classified) / 1000, where 1000 is the balanced per-class test set size.
metrics.success_threshold: All four models achieve per-class accuracy above 70% on at least 8 of 10 classes; no-augmentation condition achieves overall test accuracy >= 88% for at least one seed.

metrics.name: Per-class delta-accuracy
metrics.definition: For each class c: delta_accuracy_c = mean_accuracy_c(aug) - mean_accuracy_c(no_aug), where mean is taken across seeds 42 and 123. Reported alongside the seed-level range [min, max] as an uncertainty measure.
metrics.success_threshold: At least one class shows |delta_accuracy| > 1.5 percentage points (approximately 2.5x the binomial standard error of ~0.6pp at accuracy=0.90), indicating a non-trivial class-level effect detectable above the noise floor.

metrics.name: Per-class F1 score and delta-F1
metrics.definition: Harmonic mean of per-class precision and recall from scikit-learn for each of the four models; delta-F1 = aug_mean_F1 - no_aug_mean_F1 per class across seeds.
metrics.success_threshold: Direction of delta-F1 is consistent with direction of delta-accuracy for at least 8 of 10 classes, confirming metric coherence.

metrics.name: Delta confusion cell magnitude
metrics.definition: For each of the 100 class-pair cells (i,j) in the 10x10 row-normalized confusion matrix: delta_rate(i,j) = avg_rate_aug[i,j] - avg_rate_no_aug[i,j], where averages are taken across seeds. Diagonal cells represent per-class accuracy; off-diagonal cells represent inter-class confusion rates.
metrics.success_threshold: At least one off-diagonal cell within the confusable-tops group (T-shirt/top, Pullover, Coat, Shirt) shows |delta_rate| > 1 percentage point, consistent with the flip-induced inter-class confusion hypothesis.

metrics.name: Spearman rho: symmetry label vs. delta-accuracy
metrics.definition: Spearman rank correlation coefficient rho between the binary morphological symmetry label (1=symmetric, 0=asymmetric) and delta-accuracy across the 10 Fashion-MNIST classes, with bootstrapped 95% CI from 5,000 resamples of the 10 class data points.
metrics.success_threshold: rho > 0.2 with the bootstrapped 95% CI lower bound above -0.3, providing directional evidence for the symmetry-benefit hypothesis (noted as exploratory given n=10 classes).

datasets.name: Fashion-MNIST
datasets.role: Primary training, validation, and evaluation dataset. The 10,000-image test set with balanced 1,000-per-class structure is used for all per-class metric computation.
datasets.description: 70,000 grayscale 28x28 images of 10 balanced garment categories (T-shirt/top, Trouser, Pullover, Dress, Coat, Sandal, Shirt, Sneaker, Bag, Ankle boot): 60,000 training images split into 54,000 train and 6,000 validation, plus 10,000 test images with exactly 1,000 per class.

baselines: No-augmentation condition: SmallCNN trained with identity transforms (ToTensor and Normalize only), seeds 42 and 123, 5 epochs — primary comparator for all per-class delta computations and the pre-stated baseline for the main comparison.
Random classifier: 10% uniform per-class accuracy on the 10-class balanced Fashion-MNIST test set — lower bound for contextualising absolute per-class accuracy values.

Published SmallCNN reference accuracy: approximately 88.85% test accuracy reported for a comparable sequential CNN on Fashion-MNIST (Yee 2026) — used to contextualise whether the trained models reach expected performance levels.
plan.background: Fashion-MNIST provides ten balanced classes of 28x28 grayscale garment images as a drop-in MNIST replacement (Yee 2026), yet nearly all published CNN studies on this benchmark report only aggregate test accuracy, obscuring potentially heterogeneous per-class dynamics (Nocentini et al. 2022; Mukhamediev 2024; Xhaferra et al. 2022). Basic data augmentation — random horizontal flips, small translations, and minor rotations — is widely applied to improve CNN generalization (Greeshma et al. 2019; Shorten et al. 2019; Thanapol et al. 2020), with Fashion-MNIST state-of-the-art reaching 99.65% when augmentation and architecture optimizations are combined (Mukhamediev 2024). Fashion-MNIST contains well-documented confusable class groups (T-shirt/top, pullover, coat, and shirt share similar silhouettes (Bouzidi et al. 2026)) alongside bilaterally symmetric garments (trousers, dresses) and subtly asymmetric ones (shirts with one-sided button plackets, ankle boots with asymmetric tongues) (Yee 2026). Horizontal flip is a valid invariance for symmetric garments but may introduce label-ambiguous training examples for asymmetric items, a concern raised in augmentation theory (Lopes et al. 2021) and in flip-specific algorithmic work (Ito 2021). An analogous per-category analysis on CIFAR-10 found heterogeneous augmentation effects across classes (Agarwal et al. 2025), and class-wise augmentation studies in medical imaging demonstrate that per-class confusion patterns shift substantially depending on augmentation policy. Despite broad usage of Fashion-MNIST as a CNN benchmark (Greeshma et al. 2019; Bhatnagar et al. 2017; Kayed et al. 2020), no published work systematically decomposes augmentation impact at the per-class level, leaving it unclear whether aggregate accuracy gains mask compensating per-class losses for specific garment categories.
plan.hypothesis: Augmentation will disproportionately benefit morphologically symmetric garment classes (trousers, pullovers, dresses, coats) for which horizontal flips constitute valid invariances, while per-class accuracy may decrease for fine-grained confusable classes such as shirt versus T-shirt/top versus pullover, where flipped training images deepen inter-class confusion in the small CNN.

open_questions: Are Fashion-MNIST product images already normalized to face a canonical direction, making horizontal flip a valid invariance for all 10 classes including hypothesized asymmetric items (shirts with button plackets, ankle boots with tongues), or does the 28x28 resolution preserve visible asymmetry?

Will the SmallCNN with 3 conv blocks and 5 training epochs achieve per-class accuracy high enough (>80% for most classes) to detect class-level augmentation differences above the approximately 0.6-0.9pp binomial noise floor?

Should the train/val split use the same seed as model weight initialization (current plan) or an independent fixed split seed? The current plan maximizes within-seed consistency but conflates data-split and weight-initialization randomness.

Is the normalization Normalize(mean=0.2860, std=0.3530) the accepted standard for Fashion-MNIST, or should it be recomputed from the 54,000-sample training split to avoid slight distribution shift from the validation holdout?

Is the binary symmetric/asymmetric morphological annotation subjective enough to require independent verification, or can the agent-assigned labels be treated as ground truth for the exploratory correlation analysis?

plan.validation_strategy: Fixed 90/10 train/val split generated deterministically from each seed's torch.Generator before model initialization (54,000 train / 6,000 val / 10,000 test). Two independent seeds (42 and 123) provide modest reproducibility evidence; all per-class results are reported as mean plus seed-level range with no p-value claims, and findings are explicitly framed as exploratory throughout. Per-class accuracy estimates carry a binomial standard error of approximately sqrt(p*(1-p)/1000) ≈ 0.6-0.9pp at p=0.90, establishing an approximately 1.5pp detection threshold for meaningful class-level effects. The primary pre-stated comparison is overall test accuracy (augmented versus no-augmentation condition), and per-class analysis is a secondary exploratory decomposition. Spearman correlation across 10 class points is treated as directional evidence only. GPU execution is verified by logging the CUDA device name in environment_report.txt before any training begins.

master_plan.summary: Six agents cooperate to train SmallCNN on Fashion-MNIST under no-augmentation and augmentation conditions (seeds 42/123) and decompose accuracy by garment class. A1 implements model and training code (T1.1, T1.3, T1.4) while A2 configures data pipelines (T1.2) concurrently; A3 submits all four GPU training runs in a single run_gpu_jobs call (T2.1); A4 validates outputs and computes per-class metrics and Spearman symmetry correlation (T3.1, T4.1, T4.3); A5 merges learning curves, computes confusion matrices, and produces all figures and tables (T3.2, T4.2, T5.1–T5.4); A6 compiles all key numbers into results/SUMMARY.md (T6.1). Parallelism is maximised at three points: T1.2 and T1.3 after T1.1, T3.1 and T3.2 after T2.1, and T4.1 and T4.2 after T3.1.

execution_notes: T1.2 and T1.3 run concurrently after T1.1 (A2 and A1 in parallel) with no dependency between them.
T3.1 and T3.2 run concurrently after T2.1 (A4 and A5 in parallel); T4.1 and T4.2 run concurrently after T3.1.

All four training runs are packed into a single run_gpu_jobs call to avoid repeated queue delays; sequential execution within one GPU session is expected to take 40-50 minutes total.

The plan's T6.1 paper-draft task is replaced with a results/SUMMARY.md compilation task per blueprint rules; the Report stage handles full paper writing from this summary and the figure and table artifacts.
If torch.cuda.is_available() returns False during T2.1 GPU job execution, the script raises RuntimeError before any training begins so the job fails fast; A3 should check the log and retry.

Fashion-MNIST normalization constants mean=0.2860 and std=0.3530 are dataset-wide standard values; the slight distribution shift from the 6k validation holdout is negligible and does not require recomputation from the 54k split.
No MATLAB or non-pip tools are required; all methods are implemented with PyTorch, scikit-learn, matplotlib, seaborn, scipy, and pandas.
